title: What you could and couldn’t do

fn.en: Talk about what was and is possible, and about what you can do.

useful: It’s possible now, but it wasn’t then.

items.a: I buy bread from the baker’s
I spend a lot of money at the weekend
I do a lot of my shopping online
The shop assistant was very friendly
I can’t ski but I can swim
Thirty years ago that was impossible

items.q: A machine in the street that sells drinks: a ___ machine.
The person who buys something in a shop: the ___.
In 1970 you couldn’t buy a book at midnight. It was ___.
To talk about nothing important with the shop assistant: to ___.
The verb for using your money: to ___ it.
You do this on a website and the box arrives on Friday: you ___ it.

tts: In positive sentences and questions, can is pronounced /kən/.
Can you use euros in Norway and Sweden? I think you can use euros in Sweden, but not in Norway.
In short answers, can is pronounced /kæn/.
Can you ski? Yes, I can. Can she drive? Yes, she can.

sub.en: Look at the sentences. What is the past of can? And what form follows it?

items.q: In 1970 you ___ buy everything in one shop.
items.why: could / couldn’t is the past of can / can’t. The verb after it never changes.

items.q: Today you ___ buy almost anything online.
She ___ drive, but she can’t ski.
items.why: can never takes -s and never takes “to”.

items.q: “___ you swim?” — “Yes, I can.”
“Could people buy things online in 1990?” — “No, ___.”
In the 1970s customers ___ ask the assistant for information.
Yesterday the shop was closed, so I ___ buy any bread.
I ___ use a computer when I was ten.

acts.title: The town centre, then and now
text: THEN (the 1970s). You couldn’t buy everything from one shop. People went to the butcher’s for meat, the baker’s for bread and the newsagent’s for their newspapers. Shopping took a long time and the shops closed at five. But you could talk to the people in the shops, and they knew your name.

NOW. You can buy everything in the supermarket or the shopping centre, and you can order almost anything online. In Japan you can buy eggs from a vending machine at three in the morning. But customers can’t ask the assistant for information any more, because there often isn’t one. Nobody knows your name.

tts: People could buy things online in 1994. The first thing they could buy was pizza.
In the 1990s, rich people couldn’t buy trips into space. But in 2001 Dennis Tito paid to visit the International Space Station.
Today you can buy eggs from vending machines in Japan. And you can also buy flowers, fruit and umbrellas.
You can buy a bottle of rainwater for eleven dollars these days.

items.sit: You explain that in 1970 buying online was not possible.
o: In 1970 you couldn’t buy anything online.
In 1970 you didn’t could buy anything online.
In 1970 you can’t buy anything online.

items.sit: Someone asks: “Can you ski?” You can’t.
o: No, I can’t. But I can swim.
No, I don’t. But I can swim.
No, I couldn’t. But I can swim.

items.sit: You talk about your sister. She started driving at eighteen.
o: She could to drive at eighteen.

items.sit: You want to know if your colleague has computer skills.
o: Do you can use a computer?
Can you to use a computer?

items.sit: The baker’s was closed yesterday and you got no bread.
o: I can’t buy any bread yesterday.
I didn’t could buy any bread.

items.sit: You compare the two times in one sentence.
o: It’s possible now, but it wasn’t possible then.
It’s possible now, but it isn’t possible then.
It can now, but it couldn’t then.

write.q: Compare then and now: 6 sentences. Write three things people couldn’t do thirty years ago and three things they can do today. Then add one thing YOU can’t do.
write.model: Thirty years ago people couldn’t buy things online and they couldn’t send a photo in one second. They couldn’t work from home. Today you can order almost anything from your sofa, you can speak to somebody in another country for free, and you can pay with your phone. But I still can’t ski.

speak.q: Answer out loud: Can you drive? Can you ski? Could you swim when you were ten? Then say one thing your parents couldn’t do at your age.
speak.model: Yes, I can drive, but I can’t ski. Yes, I could swim when I was ten — my father taught me. My parents couldn’t use a computer at my age; there weren’t any.
